text: André-Marie Ampère: A Pioneering Physicist and Mathematician

André-Marie Ampère, born on January 20, 1775, in Lyon, France, was a prominent physicist and mathematician who significantly contributed to the field of electromagnetism. He is best known for his work on the theory of electric currents, which led to the adoption of the ampere, the SI unit of electric current, in his honor. Ampère's early work, including his treatise "Considerations on the Mathematical Theory of Games," showcased his prowess in mathematical probability.

Raised during the French Enlightenment, Ampère benefited from a unique educational approach inspired

tical probability.

Raised during the French Enlightenment, Ampère benefited from a unique educational approach inspired by Jean-Jacques Rousseau's philosophy. His father, Jean-Jacques Ampère, a prosperous businessman, allowed his son to educate himself using the family's extensive library. This unconventional method exposed young Ampère to seminal works such as Buffon's "Histoire naturelle" and the "Encyclopédie" by Diderot and d'Alembert. By the age of 12, Ampère had begun teaching himself advanced mathematics, mastering the works of Euler and Bernoulli in Latin. His intellectual curiosity extended beyond mathematics and science, encompassing history, philosophy, poetry, and the natural sciences.

The French Revolution significantly impacted Ampère's life. His father, a justice of the peace, was executed during the Jacobin purges in 1793. Despite this tragedy, Ampère's career flourished under the Napoleonic regime. In 1799, he secured his first regular job as a mathematics teacher, which provided him with financial stability to marry Julie Carron in 1799. Their son, Jean-Jacques Ampère, was born the following year and would later achieve scholarly acclaim in his own right.

In 1802, Ampère was appointed a professor of physics and chemistry at the École Centrale in Bourg-en-Bresse. During this period, he conducted research on mathematics, culminating in the publication of "Considerations on the Mathematical Theory of Games" in 1802. This work, submitted t

, culminating in the publication of "Considerations on the Mathematical Theory of Games" in 1802. This work, submitted to the Paris Academy of Sciences in 1803, demonstrated Ampère's early prowess in mathematical probability. Throughout his career, Ampère continued to make significant contributions to the understanding of electromagnetism, solidifying his legacy as one of the founders of classical electromagnetism.

text: Tax-Loss Harvesting Strategy in Mutual Funds

Tax-loss harvesting is a strategy that allows investors to sell securities at a loss to offset future capital gains, potentially reducing their tax liability. This strategy can be particularly beneficial for investors with mutual funds in taxable accounts. Here's how it works:

1. Identify Taxable Accounts and Mutual Funds: To engage in this strategy, you must have investments in taxable accounts, such as regular brokerage accounts, and hold mutual funds within these accounts. This strategy does not apply to tax-deferred retirement accounts like 401(k)s and IRAs, as capital gains are not taxed upon sale wi

2. Market Drops as Opportunities: When the market drops, it presents an opportunity to sell mutual funds that have decreased in value, triggering a capital loss. This loss can then be used to offset future capital gains.

3. Sell and Repurchase with a Similar but Not Identical Fund: After selling the fund at a loss, you can repurchase a similar fund immediately to maintain your market exposure. However, you must be careful not to violate the "wash sale" rule, which disallows claiming a loss on a security sold if a "substantially identical" security is bought within 31 days. To avoid this, you can buy a similar but not identical fund, such as an excha

ntical" security is bought within 31 days. To avoid this, you can buy a similar but not identical fund, such as an exchange-traded fund (ETF) with a slightly lower expense ratio.
